screens.title: Maps and Queues in the Java Collections Framework
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore two fundamental interfaces in the Java Collections Framework: Map and Queue. You will learn what makes a Map different from a Collection, how HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap organize key-value pairs, and when to pick each implementation. We’ll also look at Queue behavior, including FIFO queues implemented with LinkedList and priority-based ordering with PriorityQueue. Understanding these structures helps you choose the right tool for caching, configuration, scheduling, and queuing tasks in real applications. For example, a HashMap gives very fast lookups when order does not matter, LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order for predictable iteration or simple LRU caches, and TreeMap keeps keys sorted for range queries. For queues, LinkedList supports simple FIFO workflows like print or request queues, while PriorityQueue picks the highest-priority item first for scheduling. As we progress you’ll see concrete code examples and a small order-processing activity you can run locally. Notice common pitfalls, such as null returns from get() or needing proper equals and hashCode for custom keys. By the end you’ll be able to state when each Map or Queue choice is appropriate and how to use their main methods safely in your code.

screens.title: What is a Map?
screens.narratorSegment: A Map is a collection-like interface that stores associations between keys and values. Unlike lists or sets, a Map does not model a sequence of elements — instead each element is a mapping from a unique key to a value. This uniqueness is essential: if you put a value with an existing key, the previous value is replaced. Maps are used where you need direct lookup by name, id, or another unique identifier — think of a phone book mapping a person’s name to a phone number, or a configuration object mapping a property name to its value. Important Map methods include put to add or replace, get to retrieve a value given its key, and containsKey to check existence before using a possibly null return. Iteration helpers such as keySet, values, and entrySet let you iterate over keys, values, or both as Map. Entry objects. A common misconception is to treat Map as a Collection; because it is not, you cannot use collection semantics like positional access. Another mistake is assuming get always returns a non-null value: it returns null both when a key is absent and when a key is present with an explicit null value. A short example: using a Map to count word frequencies maps each word to its integer count and lets you increment counts quickly. Keep the equals/hashCode contract and null behaviors in mind when you design keys and consume results.

Map — core idea

screens.title: HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap
screens.narratorSegment: HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap are three common Map implementations that trade ordering for different performance and capability guarantees. HashMap uses a hash table to provide average-case constant-time operations for put, get, and remove. This makes it ideal when you need raw lookup speed and don't care about iteration order. A frequent pitfall when using HashMap is relying on unpredictable order or forgetting to implement equals and hashCode correctly for custom key types. LinkedHashMap extends the hash-based approach with a doubly linked list of entries to preserve insertion order. It is slightly slower due to the linked list overhead, but it is invaluable when you need deterministic iteration order or implement a simple LRU cache by removing eldest entries. TreeMap uses a self-balancing binary search tree under the hood, storing keys in sorted order. Its operations are logarithmic in time, which is slower than a hash table but supports range queries and retrieving smallest or largest keys easily. Note that TreeMap requires keys to be Comparable or that you provide a Comparator at construction; otherwise you’ll get runtime casting errors. When deciding, ask: do I need fastest lookups, stable insertion order, or sorted keys and range queries? That question maps directly to HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap respectively.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Map comparison
Quick comparison
HashMap
Hash table storage, average O(1) operations, no guaranteed order. Use for fast lookups where order doesn't matter.
LinkedHashMap
Hash table + doubly linked list for insertion-order iteration. Slight overhead, useful for predictable iteration and simple LRU caches.
TreeMap
Red-Black tree storage, O(log n) operations, keys are sorted. Use for range queries and ordered key retrievals.
Example scenarios
User preferences cache
HashMap gives fast access to user settings keyed by username.
LRU cache
LinkedHashMap maintains insertion/access order for simple eviction policies.
Range queries
TreeMap lets you request entries between two keys efficiently.
Common mistake: using custom objects as keys without equals/hashCode or Comparable when required.

screens.title: Map methods and iteration patterns
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson walks through the most-used Map methods and common iteration patterns. The put method inserts or updates a key-value pair; if the key already exists the old value is replaced. The get method retrieves the value for a key and returns null when the key is absent or explicitly mapped to null. To avoid ambiguity, call containsKey before using get if null is meaningful in your map. keySet returns a Set of keys, values returns a Collection of values, and entrySet returns a Set of Map. Entry objects which provide both key and value together — entrySet is often the most efficient way to iterate when you need both pieces. A concrete example: to count occurrences of words you might get the current count with get, check for null, and then put the updated count. Alternatively, Java 8 introduced computeIfAbsent and merge for concise updates, but this chapter focuses on the core methods so you understand the basics. A common misconception is iterating a Map as if it were a list; you must use keySet, values or entrySet. Practice iterating with entrySet when updating or printing both key and value to avoid extra lookups and maintain performance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Map methods
Method reference
  • put(K, V) — add or replace an entry.
  • get(Object) — return value or null if absent.
  • containsKey(Object) — test for presence before using get.
  • keySet() — iterate keys as a Set.
  • values() — iterate values as a Collection.
  • entrySet() — iterate Map.Entry for key-value pairs efficiently.
Pro tip
When you need both key and value, iterate entrySet to avoid calling get repeatedly inside the loop.
Code example
// Safely update word counts in a Map
Map<String,Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
String word = "example";
if (counts.containsKey(word)) {
  counts.put(word, counts.get(word) + 1);
} else {
  counts.put(word, 1);
}

// Iterate both key and value efficiently
for (Map.Entry<String,Integer> e : counts.entrySet()) {
  System.out.println(e.getKey() + ": " + e.getValue());
}
Key Takeaway

Prefer entrySet for key/value loops and use containsKey to avoid ambiguity from null returns.

screens.title: Queue interface and FIFO behavior
screens.narratorSegment: A Queue models a collection of elements waiting to be processed and typically follows First-In, First-Out semantics. In practical terms, the element that arrived first is removed and returned before later arrivals. Queue defines methods designed for queuing semantics: offer to add an element in a capacity-sensitive way, poll to remove and return the head or return null if empty, and peek to inspect the head without removing it. These methods are preferred in many designs because they return null or false on failure rather than throwing exceptions, which makes robust queuing code easier to write. Consider a print job queue: you offer jobs as they arrive, poll to take the next job for printing, and peek to show the next job on a dashboard without removing it. LinkedList is a common concrete implementation of Queue because of efficient additions and removals at both ends. A common misconception is confusing add/remove from Collection with offer/poll semantics; add may throw an exception on capacity failure while offer will return false. Keep the correct method set in mind to avoid surprising runtime errors in queue-backed services.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Queue basics
Queue semantics
FIFO ordering, elements wait to be processed. Use offer, poll, and peek for predictable behavior.
offer()
Add element, returns false on capacity failure instead of throwing.
poll()
Remove and return head, or null if empty.
peek()
Return head without removing it, or null if empty.
Analogy
A grocery checkout line: first customer in line is served first.
LinkedList as Queue
Because LinkedList supports fast insertions and removals at both ends, it is a natural Queue implementation. You typically declare it as Queue<T> q = new LinkedList<>();
Key Takeaway

Use offer/poll/peek for robust FIFO processing; prefer LinkedList when simple queue semantics and frequent end operations are required.

Common mistake: using add/remove and not handling exceptions on capacity failures.

screens.title: PriorityQueue: ordering by priority, not arrival
screens.narratorSegment: PriorityQueue orders its elements according to natural ordering or an explicit Comparator given at construction. Unlike a FIFO queue, the element returned by poll is the highest-priority element rather than the oldest insertion. PriorityQueue is implemented as a binary heap, which guarantees that the head is the least element according to the ordering, while the remainder of the internal structure is not fully sorted. This means you should not rely on the internal iteration order — only the head is guaranteed. Use PriorityQueue for scheduling tasks, event processing, or any situation where urgency or priority should drive processing rather than arrival time. For example, an emergency triage system could use a PriorityQueue that orders patients by severity level. Common mistakes include expecting a fully sorted list when iterating and failing to supply a Comparator or Comparable keys when needed. Also remember that if you insert custom objects, their comparison logic must be consistent with equals to avoid surprising behavior. PriorityQueue gives you efficient access to the top priority element and is a lightweight way to add priority semantics without a full sort on every operation.

keyIdea.title: Priority semantics
keyIdea.text: PriorityQueue returns the highest-priority element at the head using heap ordering. Iteration order is not fully sorted.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › PriorityQueue
How PriorityQueue works
Elements are ordered by natural ordering or a Comparator. The head is the highest priority element; the internal structure is a heap.
Use case
Task schedulers, event handlers, or triage systems where priority determines processing order.
Iteration note
Only the head is guaranteed to be the highest priority. Do not assume iteration will be sorted.
Concrete example
Imagine a PriorityQueue of tasks where a lower numeric value means higher urgency. Poll returns the most urgent task regardless of when it was added. This is ideal for processing urgent items first.
Key Takeaway

Use PriorityQueue when priority should determine processing. Remember the head is guaranteed, not full iteration order.

screens.title: Practical selection guide
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting the right Map or Queue depends on the access patterns and ordering requirements of your application. Start by asking three questions: Do I need predictable iteration order? Do I need sorted keys or range queries? Do I need priority-based processing? If you need raw lookup speed and order doesn't matter, choose HashMap for O(1) average operations. If you need insertion-order iteration or a simple LRU policy, LinkedHashMap provides a pragmatic trade-off. If sorted keys or range queries are required, TreeMap supplies O(log n) operations and direct access to smallest and largest keys. For queues, choose LinkedList for basic FIFO semantics—straightforward and efficient for head/tail operations. If processing order depends on urgency rather than arrival, use PriorityQueue and provide a Comparator if natural ordering is not available. Also evaluate mutability and concurrency needs: these implementations are not synchronized, so for multi-threaded contexts consider concurrent collections or external synchronization. Finally, remember everyday pitfalls: null behavior for get, equals/hashCode contract for hash-based maps, and Comparable or Comparator requirements for sorted maps. These checks will save production debugging time. Practical selection guide means decide by ordering needs, performance expectations, and concurrency considerations before choosing a map or queue implementation.. In practical terms, match map and queue implementations to common real-world needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Practical selection
Decision flow
Need fastest lookup and order doesn't matter: HashMap.
Need insertion order for iteration or LRU: LinkedHashMap.
Need sorted keys or range queries: TreeMap.
Need FIFO processing: LinkedList as Queue.
Need priority-based processing: PriorityQueue.
Real-world checks
  • Confirm equals/hashCode for custom keys when using HashMap/LinkedHashMap.
  • Provide Comparable or Comparator for keys in TreeMap.
  • Use offer/poll/peek to avoid exceptions in queue operations.
  • Consider synchronization or concurrent collections in multi-threaded contexts.
Common-mistake
Assuming Map iteration order is stable for HashMap or that PriorityQueue iteration is sorted.

Next the example creates a Queue using LinkedList and adds order IDs with offer. The code then polls the first two orders to simulate processing; poll returns null if the queue is empty, so the example checks isEmpty before polling. After processing, the code shows how to add a new product and update an existing price by calling put again — remember put replaces an old value if the key already exists. Finally it iterates over productPrices. entrySet to print all products, demonstrating how entrySet gives you both key and value together for efficient output. A practical point: this simple pattern maps directly to many real services where a catalog is a map and incoming requests are queued for processing. Try running the code and then modifying the queue or map updates to see how behaviour changes.

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging tips
screens.narratorSegment: When working with Maps and Queues, several recurring mistakes create bugs that are easy to avoid. First, assuming get returns a non-null value can lead to NullPointerExceptions; always check containsKey when null could be ambiguous, or use safe guards. Second, custom objects used as keys in hash-based maps must implement equals and hashCode consistently. If you fail to do this, lookups will not find previously inserted keys. Third, TreeMap requires keys to be Comparable or a Comparator supplied at construction; omitting this results in a runtime exception when comparisons are attempted. Fourth, PriorityQueue guarantees only that the head is the highest-priority element — iterating a PriorityQueue will not produce a fully sorted sequence. Fifth, prefer offer/poll/peek for queues to avoid exceptions thrown by add/remove when capacity or emptiness occur. For debugging, inspect sizes, print keySet or entrySet snapshots, and add unit tests that exercise equality and ordering assumptions. These defensive checks and small tests often catch the most subtle bugs before they reach production. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore two fundamental interfaces in the Java Collections Framework: Map and Queue. You will learn what makes a Map different from a Collection, how HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap organize key-value pairs, and when to pick each implementation. We’ll also look at Queue behavior, including FIFO queues implemented with LinkedList and priority-based ordering with PriorityQueue. Understanding these structures helps you choose the right tool for caching, configuration, scheduling, and queuing tasks in real applications. For example, a HashMap gives very fast lookups when order does not matter, LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order for predictable iteration or simple LRU caches, and TreeMap keeps keys sorted for range queries. For queues, LinkedList supports simple FIFO workflows like print or request queues, while PriorityQueue picks the highest-priority item first for scheduling. As we progress you’ll see concrete code examples and a small order-processing activity you can run locally. Notice common pitfalls, such as null returns from get() or needing proper equals and hashCode for custom keys. By the end you’ll be able to state when each Map or Queue choice is appropriate and how to use their main methods safely in your code.

By the end of the first objectives block you will be able to explain what a Map is and why its key uniqueness distinguishes it from other collections. You will also be able to name the three main Map implementations in Java — HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap — and understand their structural trade-offs. You’ll be taught the core Map methods used in day-to-day programming, including adding, retrieving, and iterating over keys and entries. Each objective includes a short rationale and a practical mnemonic to help you recall when to choose each structure. For example, knowing that a HashMap uses hashing helps you remember it is ideal for fast lookups, while LinkedHashMap’s linked order helps when iteration order matters. This screen sets outcomes you will return to as we work through examples and a small order-processing exercise. These competencies are verified milestones you can use to check your understanding as you code.

This second objectives screen focuses on applying what you learn and recognizing real pitfalls. You will practice using LinkedList as a Queue for FIFO workflows and PriorityQueue for priority-based processing. You will also learn to identify appropriate use cases for each Map and Queue implementation: when to prefer HashMap for raw lookup speed, LinkedHashMap for insertion-order iteration or simple LRU caches, and TreeMap for sorted-key operations and range queries. The objectives also emphasize two common mistakes: assuming get always returns a non-null value, and using custom objects as keys without correct equals and hashCode or without Comparable when using sorted maps. Each objective includes a small mnemonic — a line, a scale, or a sorted list — to reinforce the mental model. After completing the chapter and the hands-on order-processing task, you’ll be able to choose implementations that match both performance and ordering needs in production code.

A Map is a collection-like interface that stores associations between keys and values. Unlike lists or sets, a Map does not model a sequence of elements — instead each element is a mapping from a unique key to a value. This uniqueness is essential: if you put a value with an existing key, the previous value is replaced. Maps are used where you need direct lookup by name, id, or another unique identifier — think of a phone book mapping a person’s name to a phone number, or a configuration object mapping a property name to its value. Important Map methods include put to add or replace, get to retrieve a value given its key, and containsKey to check existence before using a possibly null return. Iteration helpers such as keySet, values, and entrySet let you iterate over keys, values, or both as Map. Entry objects. A common misconception is to treat Map as a Collection; because it is not, you cannot use collection semantics like positional access. Another mistake is assuming get always returns a non-null value: it returns null both when a key is absent and when a key is present with an explicit null value. A short example: using a Map to count word frequencies maps each word to its integer count and lets you increment counts quickly. Keep the equals/hashCode contract and null behaviors in mind when you design keys and consume results.

HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap are three common Map implementations that trade ordering for different performance and capability guarantees. HashMap uses a hash table to provide average-case constant-time operations for put, get, and remove. This makes it ideal when you need raw lookup speed and don't care about iteration order. A frequent pitfall when using HashMap is relying on unpredictable order or forgetting to implement equals and hashCode correctly for custom key types. LinkedHashMap extends the hash-based approach with a doubly linked list of entries to preserve insertion order. It is slightly slower due to the linked list overhead, but it is invaluable when you need deterministic iteration order or implement a simple LRU cache by removing eldest entries. TreeMap uses a self-balancing binary search tree under the hood, storing keys in sorted order. Its operations are logarithmic in time, which is slower than a hash table but supports range queries and retrieving smallest or largest keys easily. Note that TreeMap requires keys to be Comparable or that you provide a Comparator at construction; otherwise you’ll get runtime casting errors. When deciding, ask: do I need fastest lookups, stable insertion order, or sorted keys and range queries? That question maps directly to HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap respectively.

This lesson walks through the most-used Map methods and common iteration patterns. The put method inserts or updates a key-value pair; if the key already exists the old value is replaced. The get method retrieves the value for a key and returns null when the key is absent or explicitly mapped to null. To avoid ambiguity, call containsKey before using get if null is meaningful in your map. keySet returns a Set of keys, values returns a Collection of values, and entrySet returns a Set of Map. Entry objects which provide both key and value together — entrySet is often the most efficient way to iterate when you need both pieces. A concrete example: to count occurrences of words you might get the current count with get, check for null, and then put the updated count. Alternatively, Java 8 introduced computeIfAbsent and merge for concise updates, but this chapter focuses on the core methods so you understand the basics. A common misconception is iterating a Map as if it were a list; you must use keySet, values or entrySet. Practice iterating with entrySet when updating or printing both key and value to avoid extra lookups and maintain performance.

A Queue models a collection of elements waiting to be processed and typically follows First-In, First-Out semantics. In practical terms, the element that arrived first is removed and returned before later arrivals. Queue defines methods designed for queuing semantics: offer to add an element in a capacity-sensitive way, poll to remove and return the head or return null if empty, and peek to inspect the head without removing it. These methods are preferred in many designs because they return null or false on failure rather than throwing exceptions, which makes robust queuing code easier to write. Consider a print job queue: you offer jobs as they arrive, poll to take the next job for printing, and peek to show the next job on a dashboard without removing it. LinkedList is a common concrete implementation of Queue because of efficient additions and removals at both ends. A common misconception is confusing add/remove from Collection with offer/poll semantics; add may throw an exception on capacity failure while offer will return false. Keep the correct method set in mind to avoid surprising runtime errors in queue-backed services.

PriorityQueue orders its elements according to natural ordering or an explicit Comparator given at construction. Unlike a FIFO queue, the element returned by poll is the highest-priority element rather than the oldest insertion. PriorityQueue is implemented as a binary heap, which guarantees that the head is the least element according to the ordering, while the remainder of the internal structure is not fully sorted. This means you should not rely on the internal iteration order — only the head is guaranteed. Use PriorityQueue for scheduling tasks, event processing, or any situation where urgency or priority should drive processing rather than arrival time. For example, an emergency triage system could use a PriorityQueue that orders patients by severity level. Common mistakes include expecting a fully sorted list when iterating and failing to supply a Comparator or Comparable keys when needed. Also remember that if you insert custom objects, their comparison logic must be consistent with equals to avoid surprising behavior. PriorityQueue gives you efficient access to the top priority element and is a lightweight way to add priority semantics without a full sort on every operation.

Selecting the right Map or Queue depends on the access patterns and ordering requirements of your application. Start by asking three questions: Do I need predictable iteration order? Do I need sorted keys or range queries? Do I need priority-based processing? If you need raw lookup speed and order doesn't matter, choose HashMap for O(1) average operations. If you need insertion-order iteration or a simple LRU policy, LinkedHashMap provides a pragmatic trade-off. If sorted keys or range queries are required, TreeMap supplies O(log n) operations and direct access to smallest and largest keys. For queues, choose LinkedList for basic FIFO semantics—straightforward and efficient for head/tail operations. If processing order depends on urgency rather than arrival, use PriorityQueue and provide a Comparator if natural ordering is not available. Also evaluate mutability and concurrency needs: these implementations are not synchronized, so for multi-threaded contexts consider concurrent collections or external synchronization. Finally, remember everyday pitfalls: null behavior for get, equals/hashCode contract for hash-based maps, and Comparable or Comparator requirements for sorted maps.
